case_study_insert.main_stem: Nexa Digital Systems (NEXA) is a private limited company in the fintech and digital payments sector, supplying contactless payment software to small retailers across Ontario. Founded in 2015 by Priya Raman, NEXA employs a workforce of 60 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NEXA plans to invest $960,000 in a contactless payment platform and merchant mobile app, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $360,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $145 a unit and a selling price of $245, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. NEXA faces an operational problem: 11% of transactions last quarter were failed or delayed and merchant installers show skills gaps on the new platform.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 640 small Ontario retailers found 73% now accept contactless payments in store (up from 51% three years ago) and 61% would switch their payment provider for faster settlement. NEXA's current app takes 4.2 days to settle merchant funds; 11% of transactions last quarter were flagged as failed or delayed. Average merchant onboarding takes 5.5 days. Rival fintechs charge 2.4% per transaction while NEXA charges 2.8%. Referrals from existing merchants deliver 38% of new sign-ups; a support audit found a 1.9% repeat-contact rate on installation issues.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Nexa Digital Systems for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Technology Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate business loans and increasing merchant discount pressure. (2) The Ontario minimum wage will rise 5.8% from $16.50 to $17.46 per hour from January 2027, increasing wage costs for support and installation staff. (3) Cloud processing and data-centre costs rose 9.2% year-on-year as demand for real-time payment infrastructure grows, while Canadian digital-payment transaction volume grew 7.4% over the same period.

questions.question_text: NEXA plans to fund part of its new contactless payment platform with $360,000 of retained profit. Explain two advantages for NEXA of using retained profit instead of borrowing the full $960,000 externally.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internally generated cash, so NEXA pays no interest or capital repayments on the $360,000, protecting the cash flow that must already absorb fixed costs of $600,000 a year. Every dollar saved on interest can fund the rollout of the $960,000 contactless platform and help cover the 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs without pushing the $245 selling price above what the 640 surveyed Ontario retailers will bear, especially as rivals already charge 2.4% per transaction against NEXA's 2.8%.

Point 2: Using retained profit leaves the $600,000 ten-year bank loan as the only external claim, so Priya Raman's existing shareholders keep full ownership and control, and no lender can impose conditions on how the merchant app is built or priced. With 11% of transactions failing or delayed, NEXA needs freedom to redirect spending into fixing settlement times rather than satisfying bank covenants. Funding growth from its own trading success also signals confidence to the 61% of surveyed retailers who would switch for faster settlement, while avoiding a larger debt burden on a 60-person business.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Nexa Digital Systems and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: NEXA is launching its new contactless payment platform to Ontario retailers. Consider social media advertising, point-of-sale demonstrations in partner stores, or search-engine advertising. Which should NEXA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media advertising: Campaigns on business-focused platforms could reach thousands of Ontario retailers cheaply and let NEXA show short videos of faster settlement, appealing to the 61% of surveyed retailers who would switch providers. The weakness is poor purchase intent: most viewers are not actively shopping for payment software, so click-through is low, and the 2.8% versus 2.4% rate comparison is hard to explain in a short post. For a 60-person firm funding a $960,000 platform, broad awareness alone may not convert.

Point-of-sale demonstrations in partner stores: Demonstrating the app where retailers already shop would build trust and allow installers to answer questions about the 11% failed-transaction problem directly. It also leverages the 38% of sign-ups that come from referrals. However, coverage is geographically limited,staffing demonstrations diverts installers from onboarding that already takes 5.5 days, and reach among the 640 surveyed retailers is far too slow to drive the volume the new platform needs.

Search-engine advertising: Retailers seeking a new payment provider actively search online, so paid search reaches buyers at the moment of intent, is measurable down to cost per sign-up, and can target Ontario precisely. It lets NEXA answer the 2.4% rival price objection with the faster-settlement message of the 61% switch segment. Costs can be capped daily, protecting cash flow.

Recommendation: NEXA should choose search-engine advertising. It captures high-intent demand at controllable cost and can be scaled with the $960,000 rollout. Social media is rejected as low-intent and wasteful; in-store demonstrations are rejected as too slow and labour-intensive given the 5.5-day onboarding backlog. NEXA should add a small social layer later to build brand familiarity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NEXA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of NEXA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why social media and in-store demonstrations are rejected.

questions.question_text: NEXA's 11% failed-transaction rate and 1.9% repeat-contact rate on installation issues are damaging service quality. Explain two benefits for NEXA of using democratic leadership with its flat structure to improve performance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the installers and support staff who actually handle merchant problems to help redesign onboarding routines and the 5.5-day settlement process. In a flat structure their ideas reach Priya Raman directly, surfacing practical fixes for the 11% failed or delayed transactions that top-down instructions would miss. Being consulted satisfies esteem and belonging needs (Maslow) and acts as a Herzberg motivator, so the 60 staff are more engaged and more likely to flag faults early, protecting the 12,000 units a year of service output.

Point 2: Involvement builds ownership of the new contactless platform, reducing resistance as installers learn to use it and helping close the stated skills gaps without costly external training. Better upward communication means recurring installation faults are reported and fixed, cutting the 1.9% repeat-contact rate and safeguarding the 38% of new sign-ups driven by referrals, since satisfied merchants recommend NEXA. Higher morale also reduces the risk of staff leaving during a demanding $960,000 rollout, keeping continuity for retailers who depend on reliable payment settlement.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to NEXA's service quality, skills gaps and output.

questions.question_text: NEXA must reduce its 1.9% repeat-contact rate and 5.5-day onboarding time as the new platform rolls out. Consider expanding the in-house support team or outsourcing installation and onboarding to a specialist provider. Which should NEXA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Expanding the in-house support team: More NEXA-employed installers would understand the company's own contactless platform and could fix the 11% failed-transaction problem at source, protecting the 38% of new sign-ups generated by referrals and keeping control of merchant relationships. Training them also closes the stated skills gaps. The costs are significant: extra salaries add to fixed costs of $600,000 a year, recruitment takes time while onboarding already runs at 5.5 days, and a larger team is harder to coordinate within the flat structure.

Outsourcing to a specialist provider: An external firm could scale installers quickly without permanent wage commitments, cutting the 1.9% repeat-contact rate through specialist processes and freeing NEXA to focus on software. It would convert some fixed costs into variable ones. The drawbacks are loss of direct control over service quality, weaker knowledge of NEXA's own app, and risk to the referral engine if merchants deal with a third-party brand; hidden contract fees could also erode the $100 contribution per unit.

Decision: NEXA should expand its in-house support team, supported by targeted on-the-job training. Direct control is critical when 11% of transactions fail and 38% of growth comes from referrals, so service quality cannot be handed to an outside firm. Outsourcing is rejected because the loss of control and product knowledge would damage the very merchant relationships the $960,000 platform depends on. NEXA can still hire a small specialist firm for overflow during peak launches, but the core team should remain in-house.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to NEXA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of NEXA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of NEXA with a well-justified decision covering control, cost, service quality and skills.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NEXA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($245 − $145) = $600,000 ÷ $100 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $245 − $145 = $100. Answer: contribution per unit is $100.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NEXA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. NEXA's managers can compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 12,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 6,000 units and showing the contactless platform can absorb the enlarged fixed costs before Ontario retailer demand softens.
2. A contribution per unit of $100 lets managers model pricing, for example a 10% launch discount to $220.50 would cut contribution to $75.50 and raise break-even to about 7,947 units, so they can judge whether extra volume from the 61% switch-intent segment still covers costs.
3. Fixed costs of $600,000 and $100 contribution support the affordability test for the $600,000 ten-year bank loan and the $960,000 rollout, showing lenders repayments remain serviceable even while 11% of transactions are failing.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($600,000 ÷ 12,000 units = $50 + $145 = $195 a unit) to benchmark quarterly efficiency, target the installation problem and renegotiate cloud contracts amid 9.2% processing-cost inflation, defending the $245 price against 2.4% rivals.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $100 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 12,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $600,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $960,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $195 against 2.4% rival pricing.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NEXA's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which year shows stronger performance, and has NEXA's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.6%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 2024 = $2,400,000 − $1,440,000 = $960,000; 2025 = $2,880,000 − $1,584,000 = $1,296,000. As a share of revenue: 2024 = $960,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 40.0%; 2025 = $1,296,000 ÷ $2,880,000 = 45.0%. Operating profit as a share of revenue: 2024 = $360,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 15.0%; 2025 = $592,000 ÷ $2,880,000 = 20.6%. Returns on capital employed: 2024 = $360,000 ÷ $2,000,000 = 18.0%; 2025 = $592,000 ÷ $2,960,000 = 20.0%.

Evaluation: 2025 shows stronger performance on every measure. The share of revenue retained after cost of sales rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, reflecting better platform efficiencies and price discipline against 2.4% rivals. Capital employed grew from $2,000,000 to $2,960,000, matching the $960,000 contactless investment financed by loan and retained profit, yet returns on that larger base still improved from 18.0% to 20.0%, evidence the new capability is already earning. Operating profit rose substantially, covering interest payable rising from $48,000 to $76,000. Risks remain: 9.2% cloud-cost inflation is squeezing delivery cost, and if the 11% failed-transaction rate is not fixed, the rollout could dilute returns.

Conclusion: NEXA's financial performance has improved. Margins and returns on capital all rose, and operating profitability grew faster than revenue. The improvement is genuine, so NEXA should fix the loan rate and close the settlement problem to sustain it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether NEXA's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NEXA of launching its new contactless payment platform and merchant mobile app.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The platform directly answers the 61% of surveyed retailers who would switch for faster settlement and the 73% already accepting contactless payments, giving NEXA a differentiated product in a market where the 640-strong survey shows clear unmet demand. Faster settlement and a better app also strengthen the 38% referral engine, support the $245 price against 2.4% rivals, and help grow the 12,000 units a year that justify the $960,000 investment and improve margins.

Disadvantage: Launch quality is a serious risk: 11% of transactions are currently failed or delayed and installers show skills gaps, so a high-profile launch could magnify these faults and trigger the 1.9% repeat-contact problem across many new merchants at once. The 2.8% transaction charge is already above the 2.4% rival rate, so retailers may resist unless settlement speed is convincing, and heavy support demand during the 5.5-day onboarding period could strain the 60 staff before the platform is stable.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NEXA's research, costs and clients.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the policy rate to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs will affect NEXA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Policy rate rise to 5.00%: NEXA carries a $600,000 ten-year bank loan. If it is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% of $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $600,000 and 2025 interest payable of $76,000; if the loan is fixed-rate the direct cost is nil. Higher rates may also cool Ontario small-retailer spending on new payment systems, but NEXA can largely neutralise the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage rise of 5.8% to $17.46 per hour: The insert does not state hours worked or how many of the 60 staff are hourly-paid, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented. The honest test is productivity computed from the insert: 12,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 200 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable within a 45.0% share of revenue retained as gross profit; if installation delays reduce that productivity, unit labour costs climb and the $100 contribution per unit shrinks. NEXA can also pass part of it on given the 61% switch-intent segment.

Cloud processing cost inflation of 9.2%: This strikes every unit. The insert does not decompose the $145 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the entire variable cost rose 9.2%, it would add 9.2% × $145 = $13.34 per unit, and at 12,000 units that is roughly $160,000 a year (12,000 × $13.34). Even a fraction of that erodes the contribution underpinning the $960,000 platform, and it cannot easily be passed on to retailers already comparing 2.4% rates.

Conclusion: The 9.2% rise in cloud processing costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 units and attacks the $100 contribution that justifies the $960,000 investment; by contrast the rate rise is at most $4,500 and the wage effect cannot be quantified without invented assumptions. NEXA should lock cloud contracts and fix the loan rate.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to NEXA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NEXA's costs, demand or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of NEXA with a well-justified judgment that cloud processing cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
